title: What Does It Mean to Be Fully Prepared
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article walks through the components of genuine preparation, from setting clear goals and gathering precise information to rehearsing execution and pre-deciding contingency responses. It argues that the most overlooked element of preparation is visualization — mentally rehearsing success in vivid, multi-sensory detail — which builds both confidence and a kind of muscle memory that enhances actual performance. The piece closes by urging readers to add visualization deliberately to their preparation routine rather than treating it as optional.
points: Genuine preparation starts with clear goals and a defined strategy and tactics for achieving them.
Highly prepared performers hold themselves to a high standard of precision regarding facts, data, and background information.
Rehearsal and practice build confidence, though it's best not to schedule dry runs too close to the actual performance.
Preparation should include pre-deciding responses to likely contingencies and setbacks.
Visualization — vividly imagining success across multiple senses — is described as an underused but powerful preparation tool.
quotes: We don’t consider ourselves prepared for any event, situation, or upcoming performance until we establish the goals we want to achieve and have settled on the strategy and tactics that will enable us to succeed.
Their preparation includes knowing and understanding whatever information or facts they will need to rely on in order to succeed.
Being fully prepared also includes pre-deciding the best course of action in case things don’t go as planned.
What is less known about skilled preparation is the benefit many performers derive from visualization.
Until you can “see” what you want to have happen and the steps you need to execute to achieve your goals, you’re not completely prepared.
